lessons.title: Case Study: Four Indian Taxpayers, Four Tax Bills

body.text: The same slab table produces a zero bill, a ₹4 lakh bill and an ₹11 lakh bill. What separates them is not just income but everything around the slabs: the type of income, residential status, age, regime choice and where Total Income sits relative to each threshold.

children.text: This final lesson follows four resident taxpayers through tax year 2026-27. Each case is built to exercise a different part of the course. Try computing each bill yourself before reading the working.

cells: Nil slab, rebate, the gap between slab tax and tax payable
Regional sales head, Ludhiana, with a rented flat and a share portfolio
Heads of income, special rates, marginal vs effective rate
Retired school teacher, Thiruvananthapuram, still on the old regime
Senior citizen slabs, old vs new regime, rebate
CFO of a fintech startup, Mumbai

children.text: Ayesha joined Infosys straight from engineering college. She is on the default new regime, her taxable gross salary is ₹7,20,000 with no employer NPS, and she earns ₹6,000 of savings account interest.

cells: Less: rebate (resident, Total Income up to ₹12 lakh)

body.text: Lesson from Ayesha: slab tax of ₹12,550 is real on paper, but the rebate removes it. Her marginal rate is effectively zero, since her next ₹5,49,000 of income would still be covered. She should still file a return: it builds a filing record for future home loans and visas, and lets her claim back any TDS deducted by mistake.

children.text: Case 2: Gurpreet, Three Kinds of Income

Gurpreet heads sales for a consumer durables brand in Punjab. On the new regime, his taxable gross salary is ₹28,75,000, including ₹1,50,000 of employer NPS (within 14% of his ₹12,00,000 basic). He lets out a flat in Mohali for ₹3,00,000 a year, pays ₹20,000 of municipal tax on it and ₹1,50,000 of home loan interest. Through Zerodha he books ₹80,000 of short-term gains on listed shares and ₹2,25,000 of long-term gains on an equity mutual fund.

body.title: Working: Gurpreet's income from house property

children.text: Annual rent ₹3,00,000 less municipal tax paid ₹20,000 gives an annual value of ₹2,80,000. The flat 30% deduction for repairs is ₹84,000, leaving ₹1,96,000. Home loan interest on a let-out property is deductible under the new regime too, so subtract ₹1,50,000. Income from house property is ₹46,000. Had interest exceeded the rent, the resulting loss could not have been set off against his salary under the new regime.

cells: Tax payable, rounded to the nearest ₹10

stats.label: Marginal Rate on Salary or Rent

body.text: Lesson from Gurpreet: the gains did not push his salary into any higher slab, and each rupee of income carries a different rate depending on its type. His ₹3,05,000 of equity gains cost him ₹29,640 in tax, while the same amount of extra salary would have cost ₹95,160. For a taxpayer in the 30% slab, how income is earned matters as much as how much.

children.text: Case 3: Lalitha, the Retiree Paying Tax Out of Habit

Lalitha retired from a government school. She receives a pension of ₹5,40,000 and ₹3,10,000 of interest from the Senior Citizens' Savings Scheme and bank FDs. She has always opted for the old regime, where she claims a ₹50,000 standard deduction, ₹50,000 for senior citizen interest income and ₹50,000 for her health insurance premium.

body.title: Lalitha: Old Regime vs New Regime

columns.label: Old Regime (Senior Citizen Slabs)
points: No rebate, as income is above ₹5 lakh

body.text: Lesson from Lalitha: the senior citizen exemption limit and ₹1,00,000 of extra deductions still leave her ₹52,000 a year worse off under the old regime. Pensioners can choose their regime afresh each year when filing. Over a decade of retirement, sticking with the old regime by habit could cost her more than ₹5 lakh.

children.text: Vivaan is CFO of a Series B fintech in Mumbai, on the new regime. His basic salary is ₹18,00,000 and his taxable gross salary is ₹51,75,000, including ₹2,00,000 of employer NPS. He also earns ₹1,20,000 of FD interest. His salary alone keeps him just under ₹50 lakh; the interest pushes him over.

cells: Salary ₹51,75,000 less ₹75,000 standard deduction less ₹2,00,000 employer NPS

body.caption: Vivaan's extra ₹20,000 of income leaves him ₹800 worse off after tax

body.text: Lesson from Vivaan: he is inside the ₹50 lakh surcharge relief zone, where every extra rupee costs ₹1.04. The fix is small. His 14% employer NPS limit is ₹2,52,000, so raising the contribution by ₹20,000 to ₹2,20,000 brings Total Income to exactly ₹50,00,000. Tax falls to ₹11,23,200, a saving of ₹20,800 from moving ₹20,000 into his retirement account.

children.text: The Four Bills Side by Side

body.title: Effective Tax Rate on Total Income
Gurpreet's Rental Income
body.prompt: Suppose Gurpreet's home loan interest on the Mohali flat were ₹1,00,000 instead of ₹1,50,000, with everything else unchanged. What would his income from house property be?
body.explanation: Annual value is ₹3,00,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹2,80,000. Less 30% (₹84,000) gives ₹1,96,000. Less ₹1,00,000 of interest gives ₹96,000. This would add ₹50,000 to his slab income, costing ₹15,600 more in tax at his 31.2% marginal rate.

body.title: What Saves Lalitha ₹52,000?
body.question: Why does Lalitha pay zero under the new regime even though her Total Income there (₹7,75,000) is higher than under the old regime (₹7,00,000)?
options: Senior citizens get a higher nil slab under the new regime
The new regime rebate covers resident individuals with Total Income up to ₹12 lakh, while the old regime rebate stops at ₹5 lakh
Interest income is exempt under the new regime
Pension is not taxable under the new regime
body.explanation: The new regime has no age-based slabs, and both pension and interest remain taxable. The difference is the rebate: ₹7,75,000 is within the new regime's ₹12 lakh limit, so her ₹18,750 of slab tax is cancelled. Under the old regime, ₹7,00,000 is above the ₹5 lakh limit, so she gets no rebate at all.

body.title: The Common Thread
body.textWithBlank: In every case, the rebate test and the surcharge test are applied to ___ Income.
body.explanation: Total Income, including special-rate income and after allowed deductions, is the single figure that decides whether the rebate applies and which surcharge rate is charged.

body.title: A Fifth Taxpayer: Joseph in Doha
body.scenario: Joseph is an Indian citizen who has worked in Doha for eight years and is a non-resident for tax year 2026-27. He owns a flat in Kochi let out for ₹9,00,000 a year, with no municipal tax or home loan, and earns ₹50,000 of interest on his NRO account. He is on the new regime. His cousin, a resident with the same income, pays no tax and tells Joseph he will not either.
body.prompt: Compute Joseph's tax payable and explain why it differs from his cousin's.
body.modelAnswer: Income from house property is ₹9,00,000 less the 30% deduction (₹2,70,000) = ₹6,30,000. Adding ₹50,000 of NRO interest gives Total Income of ₹6,80,000. Slab tax is 5% of ₹2,80,000 = ₹14,000. His resident cousin's identical ₹14,000 is cancelled by the rebate, but the rebate is available only to resident individuals. Joseph pays ₹14,000 plus ₹560 cess, a total of ₹14,560. His Doha salary is not taxed in India at all because he is a non-resident. The tenant is required to deduct TDS on rent paid to a non-resident, so much of this may already have been deducted, and any excess can be claimed as a refund when he files.

body.title: Run Your Own Case Study
steps: Confirm your residential status and age for the tax year
List every source of income and put each under its head, marking special-rate income separately
Compute Total Income under both regimes, using only the deductions each allows
Apply the right slab table and special rates, then test the rebate and surcharge against Total Income
Check whether you sit in a relief zone just above ₹12 lakh, ₹5 lakh (old regime) or ₹50 lakh
Add 4% cess, compare both regimes and note your marginal and effective rates
Look for one change, such as regime choice, employer NPS or the timing of a sale, that moves you to a better position

points: Slab tax on paper and tax actually payable can be very different; the rebate, special rates, surcharge, relief and cess all sit between them
Ayesha: a resident with Total Income up to ₹12 lakh of slab-rate income pays nothing under the new regime
Gurpreet: income type matters, as equity gains carried a far lower rate than salary or rent in the same year
Lalitha: age-based old regime slabs rarely beat the new regime's ₹4 lakh nil slab and ₹12 lakh rebate for pensioners
Vivaan: small amounts of income just above a threshold can cost more than they earn, and small deductions can fix it
Joseph: residential status alone can turn a zero bill into a taxable one
Always compute Total Income first; almost every decision in the slab system is triggered by where it lands

body.text: All four cases are illustrative and use tax year 2026-27 rates for individuals. Names and employers are used for realism only; no real person's tax affairs are described. Deduction eligibility, regime switching rules and TDS obligations have conditions not fully covered here. This lesson is for education only and is not tax advice.
